sections.body: This lesson is an introduction, not a certificate. Take a hands-on first-aid course (often free or cheap from Red Cross/Red Crescent and other groups). Practice is what makes you able to help.
1. DANGER: check the area is safe for you first. 2. RESPONSE: tap the shoulders and shout 'Are you OK?'. 3. Call your local EMERGENCY NUMBER (or get someone to) and put the phone on speaker.

If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR. Push hard and fast in the centre of the chest (about 5–6 cm deep for an adult), 100–120 times a minute, letting the chest come back up between pushes.
Hands-only CPR (compressions without rescue breaths) is recommended for untrained bystanders helping an adult who collapsed. Keep going until help or an AED (defibrillator) arrives.
An AED gives spoken instructions. Turn it on and follow them. It only shocks if it detects a rhythm that needs it.
If someone is unresponsive but breathing normally, put them in the recovery position (on their side) and keep checking their breathing until help arrives.

quiz.q: You find someone collapsed. What is the FIRST thing to check?
options: That the area is safe for you
hints: You can't help if you get hurt too.
First step of DRS: D for…?
Before helping someone who fell on a busy road, you'd make sure traffic isn't coming. That's the first step.
quiz.explain: Danger first: make sure the area is safe for you before helping.

quiz.q: About how fast should chest compressions be?
hints: Many trainers use songs at about 100–120 beats per minute to keep the pace.
quiz.explain: Push at 100–120 compressions per minute, about 2 per second.

quiz.q: Someone is unresponsive but breathing normally. What should you do?
options: Put them in the recovery position and keep checking breathing
hints: CPR is for people who are NOT breathing normally.
How do you protect their airway while you wait?
If someone fainted but is breathing, you'd keep them safe and watch them, not start CPR.
quiz.explain: If they're breathing normally, use the recovery position, call for help and keep monitoring their breathing.
